title: Enforced App Control Executable, DLL, or Driver Blocks
exclusions: This use case reports Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity Operational Event 3077: the main App Control for Business enforcement-mode event stating that an executable, DLL, or driver did not pass an active policy and was blocked. It does not prove malware, tampering, an unsigned file, an invalid/revoked/expired signature, driver loading, execution success, user intent, compromise, or application outage. Event 3077 can represent an intended deny rule, an allow-policy gap, an inbox policy, Smart App Control, or multiple active policies; Microsoft documents one 3077 per policy that blocks a file. Event 3076 audit-mode “would block” records, generic Code Integrity Events 3001/3002/3004, signature/CIG Event 3033, correlated signature-detail Event 3089, policy activation failures, HVCI state, scripts/MSI/packaged apps/COM objects in the AppLocker MSI and Script channel, Sysmon image loads, and policy inventory/compliance are separate signals. The search does not alter or bypass policy and cannot establish recovery from event silence.
evidence: After deployment, retain the App Control owner and device/ring/application inventory; approved base/supplemental/inbox policy XML and binary hashes, PolicyID/GUID/name, mode, version, signer, deployment authority, rollout/change records, expected deny rules, and critical workload map; supported Windows builds/features and `CiTool -lp -json` output where available (otherwise activation/deployment inventory); locally exported 3077 and correlated 3089 XML with event version and field map; effective XML event-log input, `Splunk_TA_windows` version, deployment state, `btool`, source type/index, lag, completeness, and access controls; the `windows_appcontrol_enforcement_block` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, risk/alert records, and dashboard; each result's UTC bounds, host, blocked path, parent process, policy identity, signing levels/status, Authenticode/flat hash, ActivityID, record IDs, and raw-event reference; matching 3089 signature rows and application/process/user/download/deployment/change/EDR evidence; owner disposition, bounded exception or policy-change approval, restoration, and dated enforcement-block, audit-only, multi-policy, field-loss, collection-health, authorized-deny, allow-gap, and end-to-end controls. This documentation-only review changed no App Control policy, trust rule, code, driver, certificate, endpoint, or Splunk production configuration and created no block or alert evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest one XML-shaped CodeIntegrity/Operational event with provider `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity`, EventCode 3077, `FileName=\Device\HarddiskVolume3\Program Files\Canary\blocked-test.exe`, `ProcessName=C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe`, signing-level/status/hash fields, `PolicyName=Canary Enforced Policy`, `PolicyID=canary-policy`, `PolicyGUID={11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111}`, `ActivityID={22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222}`, and a unique record ID. Expect exactly one result with `block_events=1`, normalized paths, policy identity, both SHA-256 values, ActivityID, record ID, and `use_case=UC-1.2.60`. In the same channel, add one 3089 event with the same ActivityID and verify the triage drilldown—not the base search—returns its signature detail.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated variants and expect zero rows for Event 3076 audit-mode records; 3004/3033/3089 without a 3077; Event 3077 in the wrong channel or from another provider; Event 3077 without host or blocked-file path; AppLocker MSI and Script Event 8029; otherwise valid 3077 in the newest excluded five minutes; and a CodeIntegrity allow/activation event. Verify two 3077 events for the same file but different PolicyGUID values remain distinct groups, and companion source-health logic faults missing/stale collection or missing critical fields rather than interpreting silence as no blocks.

dataSources: Primary: Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational Event ID 3077 collected locally in XML from managed Windows devices. The local Splunk contract is `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, provider `Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity`. Required decision fields are `_time`, `dest`/`Computer`, EventCode/EventID, provider, blocked `FileName`, parent `ProcessName`, requested/validated signing levels, NT `Status`, SHA-256 Authenticode and flat hashes when present, PolicyName/PolicyID/PolicyGUID, System Correlation ActivityID, EventRecordID, source, and sourcetype. Secondary triage context is Event 3089 from the same channel, correlated one-to-many by ActivityID; each signature creates a 3089, and unsigned files produce one with TotalSignatureCount 0. Export and validate XML names per supported Windows build before relying on TA aliases.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) version 10.0.1 for Windows XML event-log collection and normalization, plus a local `windows_appcontrol_monitor` app containing the reviewed CodeIntegrity input, versioned field aliases, block search, 3089 ActivityID drilldown, source-health checks, policy/asset routing, bounded exceptions, and dashboard.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational" EventCode=3077 earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID)), dest=lower(trim(coalesce(dest,Computer,host))), provider=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName), blocked_file=lower(trim(coalesce(FileName,file_name))), parent_process=lower(trim(coalesce(ProcessName,process_name,"not_extracted"))), requested_signing_level=tostring(coalesce(RequestedSigningLevel,Requested_Signing_Level,"not_extracted")), validated_signing_level=tostring(coalesce(ValidatedSigningLevel,Validated_Signing_Level,"not_extracted")), status_code=lower(tostring(coalesce(Status,status,"not_extracted"))), sha256_authenticode=lower(tostring(coalesce(SHA256Hash,SHA256_Hash,"not_extracted"))), sha256_flat=lower(tostring(coalesce(SHA256FlatHash,SHA256_Flat_Hash,"not_extracted"))), policy_name=coalesce(PolicyName,"not_extracted"), policy_id=tostring(coalesce(PolicyID,PolicyId,"not_extracted")), policy_guid=lower(tostring(coalesce(PolicyGUID,PolicyGuid,"not_extracted"))), activity_id=lower(tostring(coalesce(ActivityID,CorrelationActivityID,Correlation_ActivityID,"not_extracted"))), record_id=tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,"not_extracted"))
| where event_code=3077 AND provider="Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity" AND len(dest)>0 AND len(blocked_file)>0
| eval block_key=coalesce(if(sha256_flat!="not_extracted",sha256_flat,null()),if(sha256_authenticode!="not_extracted",sha256_authenticode,null()),blocked_file), use_case="UC-1.2.60"
| stats earliest(_time) as first_seen latest(_time) as last_seen count as block_events values(requested_signing_level) as requested_signing_levels values(validated_signing_level) as validated_signing_levels values(status_code) as status_codes values(sha256_authenticode) as sha256_authenticode values(sha256_flat) as sha256_flat values(activity_id) as activity_ids values(record_id) as record_ids by dest blocked_file parent_process policy_name policy_id policy_guid block_key source sourcetype use_case
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| table first_seen last_seen dest blocked_file parent_process policy_name policy_id policy_guid block_key requested_signing_levels validated_signing_levels status_codes sha256_authenticode sha256_flat block_events activity_ids record_ids source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 -last_seen dest blocked_file policy_guid
description: Reports each executable, DLL, or driver that an enforced Windows App Control policy actually blocked, grouped by host, blocked path, parent process, and blocking policy. It preserves policy, signing-level, status, hash, ActivityID, and record context needed to distinguish an intended denial from a policy gap or workload-impacting rollout.
value: A block can be a successful security decision or the first evidence that a policy disrupted a required workload. Policy-grain results reduce response time by showing exactly what Windows denied, which active policy made the decision, what process requested the file, and which hash and signature-detail events must be reviewed before changing trust.
implementation: Collect CodeIntegrity/Operational in XML on every managed App Control device, validate Event 3077 and ActivityID/3089 extraction for each supported build, inventory active policies and protected workloads, and monitor channel freshness. Save the SPL as `windows_appcontrol_enforcement_block`; run every 5 minutes over the delayed closed window; route by policy/device/application; and preserve every block while deduplicating notifications. Test enforced and audit modes, multiple policies, intended denies, allow-policy gaps, field loss, lag, duplicate collection, safe policy lifecycle, application impact, and recovery. Never auto-allow a file, weaken a signer/file rule, remove a policy, or disable App Control from this event alone.
visualization: Build an App Control operations dashboard with expected-device channel freshness, field/ActivityID completeness, active-policy inventory drift, and deployment ring first; single values for blocked files, affected devices, blocking policies, and critical workloads; a timechart by policy/ring; tables for blocked path/parent/status/signing levels/hash and top repeated blocks; and policy-to-device/application drilldowns. From each row, open raw 3077, same-ActivityID 3089 signature events, policy XML/inventory, file provenance/signatures/hashes, process/user/download/software-deployment/EDR context, recent policy/application/OS changes, workload health, exception approval, and recovery. Label events as enforced policy decisions, not confirmed malware or successful driver loads.
schema: Native Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity Operational Event 3077 with ActivityID-correlated Event 3089 signature context
dataModelAcceleration: No CIM data model is claimed. CIM Change and Endpoint Processes do not preserve an App Control enforcement decision, blocking PolicyID/GUID/name, requested/validated signing levels, NT status, Authenticode versus flat hashes, or one-to-many ActivityID-correlated signature records. If scale requires summary acceleration, retain one row per raw 3077 and its full policy/file/process/hash/activity/record/source context; preserve separate 3089 rows and prove raw-to-summary parity before alerting.

knownFalsePositives:
Event 3077 is a true enforcement block under the active policy set. “False positive” therefore means the block was expected or the policy decision was operationally wrong—not that Windows fabricated the event.

1. **Approved explicit deny or vulnerable-driver block** — The policy may intentionally reject the exact file/signer/hash. Verify PolicyGUID/rule intent, file identity/hash/signatures, parent process, protected asset, approval, and absence of required-workload impact. Retain the event as proof of enforcement; suppress only duplicate notification for the exact policy and file.

2. **New or upgraded business software missing from allow rules** — A legitimate version/hash/publisher may not yet be trusted. Confirm authoritative package/source, software owner, deployment/change, signature chain and 3089 detail, expected file attributes, test results, and least-broad safe rule design. Treat as a policy gap, not permission to allow by path alone.

3. **Staged App Control enforcement-ring rollout** — Expected incompatibilities can surface as a ring moves from audit to enforce. Match device ring, exact policy version/hash, rollout ID, success criteria, rollback, owner, UTC bounds, and workload health. Preserve all blocks for rollout decisions.

4. **Multiple active policies blocking one file** — Microsoft documents a separate 3077 for each blocking policy. Several rows are distinct policy decisions, not necessarily several execution attempts. Inventory all policies and preserve PolicyGUID; fix unexpected or duplicate deployment rather than deduplicating across policy identity.

5. **Inbox policy or Smart App Control decision** — The blocking policy may not be the organization's custom base policy. Confirm policy inventory/name/GUID and supported Windows behavior before routing. Do not whitelist or remove an inbox policy based only on an assumed owner.

6. **Revoked/expired/untrusted or unsupported signature condition** — A legitimate vendor file can be blocked after certificate/reputation/policy changes. Correlate same-ActivityID 3089, 3033 when present, trusted distribution source, timestamp/chain/revocation, vendor advisory, and replacement. A valid signature alone does not prove the file should be allowed.

7. **Authorized security or application-control test** — A canary intentionally outside the policy should generate 3077. Match test ID, exact file hashes/path, parent, device/ring, policy, operator, expected count/time, alert delivery, and cleanup. Retain as control evidence.

8. **Duplicate event collection or replay** — Duplicate inputs/forwarders or restored logs can inflate `block_events`. Compare host, EventRecordID, ActivityID, event time, source/forwarder identity, input deployment, and index time; repair collection and preserve evidence of the defect.

**Safe suppression:** keep raw events and base results. Apply notification exceptions after detection through a reviewed lookup keyed to exact device/ring, PolicyGUID/version, SHA-256 flat or Authenticode hash, blocked path as secondary context, parent process when required, change/test/deny-rule ID, owner/approver, and exclusive epoch bounds. Reject filename-only, publisher-wide, path-wildcard, policy-wide permanent, device-wide, or blanket maintenance exclusions. Never suppress unknown policy drift, critical workload impact, blocked Windows/security agents, hash/signature mismatch, unexpected parent/user/download, repeated blocks after approved rollout, missing 3089/context fields, or stale/missing CodeIntegrity collection.
hardware: Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server 2016 or later devices using App Control for Business, subject to Microsoft's version-specific feature table. CiTool inventory is available only on documented newer releases; older systems require their supported policy-deployment and activation-event inventory path.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against Microsoft App Control event-ID/tag, troubleshooting, deployment, feature, CiTool, trust-rule, and audit-to-enforcement guidance plus Splunk Windows XML event-log/add-on documentation; Windows-build XML templates, TA aliases, policy inventory, fixtures, code/signatures, blocks, workload impact, alert delivery, exception design, policy remediation, and recovery were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Windows/App Control/application/Splunk/security SME-signed

cost.search_load_notes: The base search scans one low-volume enforcement event ID from one operational channel over a closed five-minute window. Signature Event 3089 is retained for drilldown rather than joined into the alert, avoiding one-to-many inflation. Source-health, missing-field, policy-inventory, and retention controls remain mandatory.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact enforcement claim

Assign App Control policy, Windows endpoint/server, security, application/software packaging, certificate/signing, deployment-ring, EDR, Splunk collection/content, telemetry-health, and incident owners. Inventory every managed device/build/edition/ring and protected workload; expected base, supplemental, deny-only, inbox, and Smart App Control policies; PolicyID/GUID/name/version/hash/mode/signer/deployment authority; trust/deny-rule intent; critical executables/DLLs/drivers and service/boot dependencies; exception authority; rollback; and recovery transaction. Microsoft supports App Control across Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2016+, but capabilities vary. Record the applicable feature table rather than promising one procedure on every release.

Microsoft defines CodeIntegrity Operational Event 3077 as the main enforcement-mode block event for executables, DLLs, and drivers: the file did not pass a policy and was blocked. That is the only detection claim. Do not relabel 3001 as “blocked driver,” 3033 as generic “unsigned image loaded,” or 3002/3003/3004 as interchangeable App Control enforcement. Event 3076 means would-have-blocked in audit mode and must remain a rollout signal, not an actual block. Scripts, MSI, packaged apps, and COM objects use the AppLocker MSI and Script channel and different events/semantics.

A 3077 does not identify maliciousness or cause by itself. The blocked file can fail an explicit deny, allow-list, signer, file-attribute, hash, reputation/ISG, inbox, or other active policy condition. Microsoft documents one 3077 per blocking policy, so policy identity belongs in the alert grain. Event 3089 carries one row per discovered signature and correlates through System Correlation ActivityID; an unsigned file still has one 3089 with TotalSignatureCount zero. Preserve this one-to-many context outside the base aggregation.

## Step 1 — Validate policy and XML telemetry

Before enforcement monitoring, export the approved policy XML and binary, calculate hashes, record deployment method/ring/change, and confirm policy inventory. On versions with inbox CiTool (Microsoft documents Windows 11 22H2+ and Windows Server 2025), collect `CiTool.exe -lp -json` and inspect Is Currently Enforced/authorized and policy IDs. On earlier systems, use the supported deployment authority, policy files and CodeIntegrity policy-activation events such as 3099; do not claim CiTool availability. Compare expected and actual base/supplemental/inbox policies and alert unknown, missing, duplicate, wrong-mode, or wrong-version policy separately.

On a canary for each supported Windows build, export one redacted 3077 and its same-ActivityID 3089 XML from `Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft\Windows\CodeIntegrity\Operational`. Record provider/channel/EventID/Version; System Correlation ActivityID; blocked FileName; ProcessName; requested/validated signing levels; NT Status; Authenticode and flat SHA-256 hashes; PolicyName/ID/GUID; resource attributes; and EventRecordID. Microsoft notes that on-disk File Name is mutable and OriginalFileName is the resource attribute used by the FileName rule level by default. Validate exact EventData names and TA aliases; keep a versioned fixture contract.

Deploy or merge one local input—never duplicate an existing channel stanza:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational]
disabled = 0
renderXml = 1
index = wineventlog
```

Use the Universal Forwarder and Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) deployment appropriate to the platform. Splunk documents XML event collection and `$XmlRegex` behavior if input filtering is applied. Ensure 3077, 3076, 3089, 3099, and needed health/context events survive any allowlist. Verify `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, app precedence, service identity, `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-CodeIntegrity/Operational`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, index routing, permissions, event lag, and XML fields. Restrict access because paths, policy names, hashes, users, and certificate details are sensitive.

Build companion health checks for expected device with no recent channel event/heartbeat; missing EventCode/provider/path/policy/ActivityID/hash extraction; unknown event version; duplicate EventRecordID; future/late time; host identity drift; TA/input drift; duplicate collectors; channel disabled/cleared; and expected-policy inventory mismatch. Event silence is not proof that enforcement is active, correctly deployed, or block-free. Event 3099/policy inventory and tested canary blocks provide control-state evidence.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the block search

Save as `windows_appcontrol_enforcement_block`; schedule every 5 minutes. At 12:15, `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` evaluates 12:05–12:10 and leaves five minutes for collection. Measure p95/p99 lag and move both bounds together. A single 3077 is reportable; this is not a frequency threshold. Route/block severity by policy, device ring, file classification, parent, critical workload impact, and whether the deny was expected. Preserve base events even if notification is throttled.

The first stage uses exact source/sourcetype/EventCode predicates. `eval` normalizes host/provider, blocked and parent paths, signing levels, NT status, Authenticode/flat hashes, policy identity, ActivityID, and record ID. Local field aliases cover validated TA naming only; missing context remains `not_extracted` rather than invented from Message. `where` requires the exact Microsoft provider, host, and blocked path. Missing policy/hash/ActivityID does not erase a confirmed 3077 but must trigger field-health investigation.

`block_key` prefers SHA-256 flat hash, then Authenticode hash, then path; this is a routing identifier, not proof of file equivalence. `stats` groups by host, blocked path, parent and full policy identity, so multiple active policies remain separate. It retains all levels/statuses/hashes/ActivityIDs/record IDs. `block_events` can be repeated attempts or collection duplicates; inspect record/activity identity. No join to 3089 is performed in the alert because each signature generates a row and an unsigned file still has a row; an unrestricted join can inflate or discard blocks. A drilldown searches the same channel for `EventCode=3089 ActivityID=<selected>` in a tight time range and presents all signature records.

Do not supply a CIM/tstats “equivalent.” A generic Change or Process row cannot assert an enforced policy block or preserve policy/signing evidence. If summary acceleration is required, compare every raw 3077 to one summary row and retain raw links and separate signature detail.

## Step 3 — Validate enforcement semantics and safe operations

Create redacted XML fixtures from locally exported events. Test one and repeated 3077; 3076 audit-only; 3004/3033/3089 alone; different providers/channels; empty path; missing policy/hash/ActivityID; user executable, DLL and lab driver paths; parent `System`; mixed case; multiple policies for one ActivityID/file; multiple signatures/3089 rows; unsigned 3089 zero-signature case; duplicate record; newest-window exclusion; late arrival; and exact earliest/latest boundaries. Assert output grain, block key preference, no signature inflation, and all evidence columns. Test source/field/policy health separately.

Use Microsoft-recommended deployment rings: audit first, review 3076 and AppLocker script/MSI signals, then enforce only after success criteria. In an isolated canary policy/ring, use a benign signed test executable that is deliberately outside trust or explicitly denied. Record file hashes/source, policy XML/binary hash, device, change/test ID, expected policy and ActivityID. Confirm Windows refuses it, 3077 and correlated 3089 appear, Splunk ingests both, the search returns one policy-grain row, routing fires, and the owner acknowledges. Remove only the authorized canary/test rule or restore the supported test state, then prove the intended application works and policy remains enforced.

Test an approved business-app upgrade missing from audit rules, an intended deny, multiple active policies, device ring transition, policy rollback, inbox policy, critical service/boot dependency in a disposable lab, duplicate collection, missing ActivityID, and channel outage. Never test by blocking a production boot-critical driver, security agent, storage/network component, or Splunk forwarder. Verify notification exceptions do not hide an unknown policy, changed hash, different parent, different device/ring, critical workload impact, or post-window blocks.

Measure event/byte rate, field completeness, ActivityID-to-3089 ratio, policy cardinality, collection lag, search runtime, alert latency, intended-deny rate, allow-gap rate, owner response, workload impact, and recovery. Record OS/forwarder/TA/Splunk versions, policy/device/ring, XML fixture and binary/file hashes, search SID, dispatch/alert/case IDs, exact UTC bounds, expected/actual rows, policy disposition, and recovery evidence. Keep `draft` until Windows/App Control, application, security, and Splunk owners sign the tested contract.

## Step 4 — Triage, policy decision, and response

For each result: (1) verify raw 3077 provider/channel/version, host/time/record and collection health; (2) identify blocked file and parent, but do not execute or copy it casually; (3) inventory all active policies and match PolicyGUID/ID/name/version/hash to the approved deployment/ring; (4) retrieve all same-ActivityID 3089 signatures and related 3033/other events; (5) interpret requested/validated signing levels and NT Status using Microsoft's event-tag/troubleshooting guidance; (6) verify Authenticode and flat hashes, resource attributes, signer chain/timestamp/revocation and authoritative package provenance in a safe analysis path; (7) correlate process/user/session, download/email/browser/software deployment, EDR, vulnerability and change evidence; and (8) test the owning application/service transaction and assess boot/security/control impact.

Classify the outcome: intended deny/control success; authorized canary; expected ring incompatibility; legitimate software policy gap; unexpected/duplicate/wrong policy; suspicious/unapproved file; signature/revocation/vendor problem; or collection/schema defect. A valid signature does not automatically make code trusted, and an unsigned file is not automatically malicious. Event 3077 confirms policy enforcement, not the exact trust-rule failure; use policy and 3089 evidence.

Escalate immediately for blocked boot/storage/network/security/identity/backup/monitoring components, widespread critical application failure, unexpected policy/ring drift, repeated unknown binaries, high-risk parent/user/download chain, hash/signature mismatch, new deny affecting many hosts, or a policy apparently deployed to cause denial of service. Preserve policy binary/XML, logs, file metadata and volatile endpoint evidence before changes.

Never automatically create a hash/path/publisher allow rule, trust a certificate, disable UMCI/script enforcement, switch policy to audit, remove an inbox/base policy, delete policy files, run CiTool update/remove, disable Code Integrity/HVCI, reboot, or bypass the file. Microsoft warns App Control changes can have unintended consequences and prescribes version/deployment-specific lifecycle actions. The policy owner must choose the narrowest supported signer/file-attribute/hash rule or rollback after source/signature/application validation, peer review, testing, and approval. Hash rules change with every binary update; path/publisher rules can be dangerously broad. Follow signed-policy removal/reboot requirements for the actual version.

Recovery requires more than no new 3077. For an allow gap, prove the approved policy version is active, the exact trusted software starts, its transaction succeeds, no broader code gained trust, and the block does not recur. For intended deny, prove the file stayed blocked or was removed/quarantined under response authority and the protected workload remains healthy. For wrong-policy deployment, prove expected policy inventory and enforcement after rollback. Keep source-health green throughout.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot

- **No 3077:** verify an enforced App Control policy actually applies, policy inventory/3099, canary behavior, channel enabled, input/forwarder, `btool`, source/sourcetype/index, role access, XML filtering, lag and time bounds. Audit mode produces 3076 instead.
- **3076 but no 3077:** expected in audit mode. Do not relabel would-have-blocked as blocked; review readiness and deployment mode.
- **Script/MSI block absent:** inspect AppLocker MSI and Script events (for example 8029) and script-host semantics. CodeIntegrity 3077 covers executables/DLLs/drivers, not the entire script pipeline.
- **Policy fields missing:** compare raw XML event version/build with fixture and TA alias precedence. Keep `not_extracted`, raise field health, and update/test aliases; do not parse localized rendered Message as the primary contract.
- **ActivityID/3089 missing:** inspect System Correlation attribute, XML rendering/filtering, time bounds, event version and channel retention. Do not infer signer state from 3077 alone.
- **Several rows for one file/time:** inspect PolicyGUID; Microsoft emits one block per blocking policy. Also check duplicate EventRecordID/collector before deduplication.
- **Different SHA-256 values:** Authenticode and flat hashes are different constructions. Preserve labeled fields; never compare one type to the other as if equal.
- **Path looks like `\Device\HarddiskVolume...`:** this is valid native device-path context. Resolve to a volume only during triage and retain original path; do not make permanent path exceptions from a mutable mapping.
- **Policy inventory differs from event:** inspect deployment authority, multiple/inbox policies, stale/duplicate binary locations and activation events using Microsoft guidance. Treat unknown active policy as high risk.
- **Allowed rule added but still blocked:** another active policy can still block the file; inspect every policy-grain 3077, policy deployment/activation, exact file/hash/signer attributes and supported update/reboot requirements.
- **Block stopped but app still fails:** verify application/service/process and dependent script/MSI/COM/driver events. Event silence is not transaction recovery.
- **Channel floods:** identify repeated legitimate launch loops or multi-policy events, fix application/policy cause, and throttle notification by exact file/policy/device—not ingestion or raw evidence.
grandmaExplanation: Windows can enforce a list of programs and drivers that are allowed to run. When it actually stops a file, we show the team which file was blocked, which program tried to use it, and which policy made the decision so they can tell protection from an accidental business outage.
